C005.subject: GDP per capita
C005.object: reported life satisfaction in high-income countries above $50,000 PPP
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita reported life satisfaction in high-income countries above $50,000 PPP]

[PATH:empirical] World Happiness Report panel data (2005-2023) with GDP per capita (PPP) and life satisfaction scores for high-income countries — Directly tests the hypothesized negative correlation above $50,000 PPP by analyzing within-country and cross-country trends, controlling for confounders like inequality and social support.

[PATH:literature] Kahneman & Deaton (2010) 'High income improves evaluation of life but not emotional well-being' and subsequent replications focusing on high-income thresholds — Established the classic satiation point; re-examining with updated data and higher thresholds can confirm or refute whether the negative trend emerges beyond $50,000.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey of work stress, social comparison, and life satisfaction in countries like the US, Switzerland, and Norway (e.g., German Socio-Economic Panel or Swiss Household Panel) — Tests the proposed causal mechanisms (work stress, social comparison) that could explain a negative correlation, providing mechanistic evidence rather than just correlational.

qualifier.caveat: beyond $50,000 PPP, higher GDP per capita is associated with lower life satisfaction due to increased work stress and social comparison

C006.subject: Social and cultural factors
C006.object: reported life satisfaction in high-income countries
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Social and cultural factors reported life satisfaction in high-income countries]

[PATH:empirical] World Values Survey (WVS) panel data for high-income countries (2000-2020), analyzing the explanatory power of cultural values vs. GDP per capita on life satisfaction — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing variance explained by social/cultural indicators (e.g., trust, individualism) against economic factors in a cross-national time-series design.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on subjective well-being determinants in OECD countries, focusing on the relative effect sizes of cultural norms vs. income — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether social/cultural factors consistently show stronger associations than economic variables across multiple high-income contexts.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal natural experiment comparing life satisfaction trends in high-income countries with rapid cultural change (e.g., Japan, South Korea) versus stable cultural contexts (e.g., Nordic countries) — Exploits variation in cultural shifts to isolate causal influence of social/cultural factors, controlling for economic growth.

C007.subject: Alternative metrics (e.g., HDI, GPI) augmented with participatory wellbeing assessments
C007.object: subjective dimensions of wellbeing (e.g., community, autonomy) more accurately across cultures than standard alternative metrics alone
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Alternative metrics (e.g., HDI, GPI) augmented with participatory wellbeing assessments subjective dimensions of wellbeing (e.g., community, autonomy) more accurately across cultures than standard alternative metrics alone]

[PATH:empirical] Multi-country participatory wellbeing studies (e.g., WeD, OECD Better Life Index local adaptations) — Directly compares standard alternative metrics (HDI, GPI) against those augmented with participatory assessments (e.g., community voice, autonomy scales) across diverse cultural contexts in low- and middle-income countries, testing whether augmented metrics reduce cultural bias.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of cross-cultural validity of subjective wellbeing dimensions (e.g., autonomy, relatedness) in global surveys (e.g., World Values Survey, Gallup World Poll) — Synthesizes existing evidence on whether participatory methods capture culturally specific dimensions of wellbeing that standard metrics miss, providing statistical confirmation or refutation of differential accuracy.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental field studies comparing participatory wellbeing assessment methods (e.g., Most Significant Change, wellbeing ranking) with conventional survey-based alternative metrics — Tests causal claim by randomly assigning communities to standard vs. augmented measurement and evaluating criterion validity against ethnographic benchmarks, offering high internal validity for the hypothesis.

qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on low- and middle-income countries

C008.subject: Alternative metrics (e.g., HDI, GPI)
C008.object: essential aspects of subjective wellbeing (e.g., community, autonomy)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Alternative metrics (e.g., HDI, GPI) essential aspects of subjective wellbeing (e.g., community, autonomy)]

[PATH:empirical] World Values Survey (WVS) and Gallup World Poll data on subjective wellbeing, correlated with HDI and GPI scores across countries (2000-2020) — Provides cross-national quantitative data to test whether alternative metrics like HDI and GPI align with self-reported measures of community, autonomy, and other subjective wellbeing dimensions, especially comparing Global North and South.

[PATH:theoretical] Qualitative case studies from Bhutan's Gross National Happiness (GNH) index and Latin American 'Buen Vivir' frameworks — Offers theoretical and contextual insights into how non-Western conceptions of wellbeing (community, autonomy) are operationalized, challenging or supporting the adequacy of HDI/GPI in capturing these aspects across cultures.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of literature on alternative metrics and subjective wellbeing (e.g., OECD Better Life Index, Happy Planet Index) in cross-cultural settings — Synthesizes existing empirical findings and theoretical critiques to evaluate the overall evidence on whether these metrics capture essential subjective dimensions, identifying gaps and contradictory results.
